# Modes of underwater diving
Underwater diving refers to human activity underwater with or without special breathing equipment. The modes of underwater diving are commonly classified by the method the diver uses to remain underwater and whether the diver is exposed to the ambient water pressure. The two broad categories are ambient pressure diving, where the diver’s body is at the same pressure as the surrounding water, and atmospheric pressure diving, where the diver is inside a pressure-resistant suit or vehicle and remains at normal surface pressure. Within ambient pressure diving, the main modes include breath-hold diving (freediving) without any breathing apparatus, SCUBA diving using self-contained breathing gas equipment, and surface-supplied diving where the diver is connected to a surface air supply via an umbilical hose. In contrast, atmospheric pressure diving employs rigid armored suits that keep the diver at one atmosphere of internal pressure, enabling very deep dives without the physiological hazards of high ambient pressure. Each mode of diving has distinct techniques, applications, advantages, and limitations, which are described below.
## Breath-hold diving (Freediving)
Freediving is underwater diving on a single breath of air, without using any breathing apparatus. The diver inhales at the surface and then holds their breath for the duration of the dive, resurfacing before breathing again. Because there is no external air supply, freediving dives are typically short in duration and relatively shallow, but skilled freedivers can achieve remarkable depths and times. Modern competitive freedivers, using specialized training and techniques, have reached depths well over 100 meters on one breath. (In 2007, for example, a record “no-limits” dive reached 214 m in depth.) In practice, recreational and competitive freediving disciplines often involve dives of tens of meters in depth, and static breath-holds lasting several minutes.
Freediving is the oldest form of diving and has been practiced by humans for thousands of years for food gathering, pearl diving, and sponge harvesting. For instance, in Japan the traditional Ama divers (often women) have been freediving for over 2,000 years to collect shellfish and pearls, commonly diving to depths of 5–10 meters and sometimes up to 20 meters on a single breath. Around the world, many cultures developed breath-hold diving techniques for fishing and harvesting resources long before modern diving technology. Today, freediving is not only a method for spearfishing and underwater recreation but also a competitive sport in its own right, with disciplines such as constant weight, free immersion, and dynamic apnea. Because freedivers are under ambient pressure and breathe no compressed gas, they avoid certain risks like decompression sickness, but they face others such as hypoxic blackout (loss of consciousness from lack of oxygen). Careful training, gradual depth progression, and the use of a buddy system are critical safety practices in freediving.
## Scuba diving
Scuba diving is a mode of underwater diving in which the diver uses a self-contained underwater breathing apparatus (scuba) to breathe from a compressed gas supply carried on their person. In scuba, the diver typically wears one or more high-pressure cylinders filled with breathing gas (usually compressed air or nitrox) and breathes through a demand regulator mouthpiece. This apparatus allows the diver to swim freely without any tether to the surface, making scuba diving popular for recreation, scientific exploration, and underwater work in moderate depths. The word SCUBA is an acronym for “Self-Contained Underwater Breathing Apparatus”, reflecting that all necessary gas supply and breathing equipment travels with the diver.
A standard scuba setup is an open-circuit system: each breath the diver takes from the tank is exhaled into the water as bubbles. Open-circuit scuba is mechanically simple and very common, but it wastes the portion of oxygen that the diver does not metabolize. An alternative is the closed-circuit or semi-closed rebreather, which retains the diver’s exhaled gas, removes the carbon dioxide, and replenishes oxygen, allowing the gas to be recycled for further breathing. Rebreather systems greatly extend the underwater duration for a given gas supply and produce few or no bubbles (useful for stealth or wildlife observation), but they are complex and require careful monitoring of the gas mixture to avoid hypoxia or oxygen toxicity. Scuba equipment can use a variety of breathing gases depending on the dive requirements: air (21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen) is standard for recreational dives, while enriched air nitrox (with higher oxygen fraction) is used to extend no-decompression limits at moderate depths. For deep or technical dives beyond about 40 meters, mixtures like trimix (oxygen, nitrogen, and helium) or heliox (helium and oxygen) are used to reduce nitrogen narcosis and manage oxygen exposure. These mixed-gas techniques fall under technical diving and require special training. Overall, scuba diving enables a high degree of mobility and autonomy underwater, but dive depth and duration are limited by the amount of gas the diver can carry and by physiological constraints such as decompression requirements. Scuba divers must ascent at a controlled rate and often perform safety stops (or staged decompression stops on deeper dives) to let dissolved inert gas escape safely and avoid decompression sickness.
## Surface-supplied diving
Surface-supplied diving is a mode where the diver’s breathing gas is provided from the surface, through a hose (or bundle of hoses) known as an umbilical. Unlike scuba divers who carry their own cylinders, a surface-supplied diver is tethered to a support station (such as a dive boat or shore facility) that pumps air or mixed gas down to the diver continuously. This arrangement typically involves the diver wearing a helmet or full-face mask connected to the umbilical, and a communications line to talk to the surface team. Surface-supplied diving is the standard method for most commercial, military, and other professional diving work, especially for long-duration tasks or deeper dives. It originated with the classic “hard hat” divers of the 19th century and has evolved with modern helmets and deck decompression chambers.
Surface-supplied systems have several advantages over scuba for industrial use. First, the gas supply is essentially unlimited – the diver can remain underwater for extended periods without worrying about running out of air. This makes it practical to undertake lengthy underwater construction projects, inspections, welding, salvage operations, and other tasks that would be impossible on a single tank of air. Second, the tether provides a lifeline and communication link that enhances safety. The surface support team can monitor the diver’s status and speak to them, and they can assist or immediately pull up the diver in an emergency. Constant communication and topside monitoring significantly reduce the risk of the diver becoming lost or incapacitated without help. Because the diver’s return to the surface can be controlled by the surface crew (e.g. via a winch on a stage or the umbilical), there is an added layer of safety and coordination. Surface-supplied divers also typically carry a backup emergency gas supply (a “bailout bottle”) on their harness in case the main hose supply is interrupted.
This mode of diving does come with trade-offs. The diver’s range of movement is limited by the length and management of the umbilical hose, which can be cumbersome and requires diligence to avoid entanglement. The equipment (helmets, umbilicals, compressors or gas cylinders, etc.) is heavy and expensive, and thus surface-supplied diving is generally not used for casual or recreational purposes. It is primarily employed in professional contexts where the infrastructure and support personnel are available. Surface-supplied divers must follow careful procedures for decompression when surfacing from deeper or long-duration dives, often using on-site decompression chambers to safely eliminate inert gases from their body after a dive. Standard surface-supplied “air diving” is usually limited to relatively shallow depths (often up to about 50–60 m) due to the increasing risk of nitrogen narcosis and oxygen toxicity; for greater depths, surface-supplied systems can be used with helium-based mixed gases (surface-supplied mixed-gas diving) to extend depth range.
Saturation diving. In commercial projects that require very deep dives or many hours of work at depth, surface-supplied diving is often combined with saturation diving techniques. Saturation diving is a special mode in which divers live under high pressure in a sealed chamber for days or weeks, so that their bodies become fully saturated with inert gas at the working depth. Once saturation is achieved, the time required for decompression does not increase with additional time spent underwater – the divers will need the same lengthy decompression regardless of whether they spend one day or several days working at depth. The major benefit is that the divers can perform long shifts of work each day (transported to and from the underwater work site via a pressurized diving bell) and then only undergo a single, carefully managed decompression procedure at the end of their tour (instead of decompressing after every dive). Saturation divers live in a pressurized habitat (either an underwater habitat or more commonly a deck-mounted chamber on a ship) at the pressure equivalent of the work depth, and are supplied with breathing gas and essentials through that habitat. They typically breathe a heliox mixture (helium–oxygen) when at great depth, since using air would cause severe narcosis and other issues – depths below about 50–60 m generally require replacing nitrogen with helium. For example, saturation divers working around 200 m depth breathe heliox from the surface supply; at such extreme pressures a small percentage of nitrogen might be added to heliox to mitigate the effects of High-Pressure Nervous Syndrome (HPNS), a trembling condition caused by high-pressure helium. Saturation diving is logistically complex and very costly, but it enables humans to operate at depths of several hundred meters. The deepest experimental saturation dive conducted reached a pressure equivalent to 701 m of seawater (a 1992 Comex experiment) – an extreme record. In practice, commercial saturation dives are commonly done in the range of 100–300 m for offshore oil, gas, and salvage work. This mode carries significant risks, and operations are conducted with a large support crew and strict procedures to ensure the health and safety of the divers.
## Atmospheric pressure diving
Beyond the limits of ambient pressure techniques, humans can also dive using systems that keep the diver at one atmosphere of internal pressure regardless of external depth. In this mode, often called atmospheric diving, the person is enclosed in a stiff, pressure-resistant suit or vehicle that prevents the ambient water pressure from affecting their body. The most prominent example is the Atmospheric Diving Suit (ADS) – a specialized armored suit that a diver wears to achieve great depths. An ADS is essentially a one-person articulated submersible shaped like a suit of armor, with movable joints that maintain a sealed internal pressure of 1 atm. The suit contains an oxygen supply and CO₂ scrubbers to sustain the occupant, and often battery-powered thrusters or it may be connected to the surface by an umbilical for power and communication. Because the diver inside remains at normal pressure, they do not need to decompress when the ADS is brought back to the surface, and they are not subject to depth-related problems like nitrogen narcosis or decompression sickness. This allows atmospheric diving suits to be used for very deep dives far beyond the depths reachable by unprotected divers. Modern ADS designs (such as the JIM suit, Newtsuit, or the Exosuit) have operational depths on the order of 600–700 m (around 2,000+ feet), and they enable dive durations of many hours since life support can be maintained without the limitations of a human body under pressure.
Atmospheric diving suits are employed for specific tasks like deep ocean oil rig maintenance, submarine rescue, scientific sampling, or recovery operations at extreme depths. They combine some of the access and dexterity of a human diver (with manipulators that can use tools) with the pressure immunity of a submersible. However, ADS units are highly specialized and expensive pieces of equipment, and they are bulkier and less maneuverable compared to a free-swimming diver. The suit’s joints and life-support systems also impose practical limits on mobility and endurance. For even larger-scale or longer-duration deep missions, crewed submersibles (mini-submarines) or remotely operated vehicles are used rather than atmospheric dive suits. Those craft, like an ADS, maintain an internal one-atmosphere environment, but they are usually not considered “modes of diving” in the same sense, since the occupants do not directly contact the water. In summary, atmospheric pressure diving via suits allows humans to extend their underwater reach to depths otherwise inaccessible, by eliminating the physiological stresses of high-pressure exposure. This mode complements the ambient-pressure diving modes, each being suitable for different depth ranges and purposes.

[History of Freediving is part of the Beginners Guide to Freediving](https://www.deeperblue.com/beginners-guide-freediving/)

Freediving is as old as humanity’s relationship with the sea. For millennia, people have held their breath to dive for food, gather materials, wage war, or explore. What began as a necessity of survival has evolved into a sport that combines science, discipline, and adventure.

This chapter traces the arc of freediving’s history – from ancient sponge divers to modern world champions – and explores how humans continue to push the boundaries of physiology and performance underwater.

Key Takeaways
-------------

*   Freediving dates back thousands of years, with records from Greece, Japan, Korea, and the Pacific.
*   Divers once harvested sponges, pearls, and shellfish, or served navies as saboteurs and salvagers.
*   The 20th century saw freediving shift from necessity to structured sport.
*   Innovations such as masks, fins, and wetsuits transformed what was possible.
*   Pioneers like Enzo Maiorca, Jacques Mayol, and Natalia Molchanova set the stage for today’s champions.
*   World records now exceed **130 m (426 ft)** in Constant Weight and **214 m (702 ft)** in No Limits.

Ancient Freediving Traditions
-----------------------------

In terms of our more recent history, we know for a fact that humans have been freediving for food for at least 8,000 years.

Archaeologists investigating the mummified remains of the Chinchorian, an ancient peoples that lived circa 6,000BC in what is today Chile, found them to have suffered from exostosis, the condition where the bones of the ear canal start to grow across the opening to help protect the eardrum from repeated exposure to cold water. It’s a condition known in modern parlance as ‘surfers ear’, though divers, surfers, and kayakers are equally likely to suffer from it – as is anyone who’s repeatedly dunked underwater.

The Chinchorian and their ilk weren’t freediving for pleasure, though, but for food and goods to trade. Pearls and sponges were among the first underwater items to find value amongst in-land societies and those without the skills with which to dive for them.

In 332 BC, Alexander the Great famously used freedivers to dismantle the underwater booms preventing his ships from entering the harbor during the siege of Tyre.

### Greece and the Mediterranean

Some of the earliest written accounts come from **ancient Greece**, where sponge and pearl divers worked for trade and naval uses. Divers in the Aegean are recorded as early as 4,000 years ago.

*   The **“skandalopetra” stone** – a flat rock weighing 8-14 kg – was used by divers to descend quickly, then hauled up by rope.
*   Sponge divers in **Kalymnos** became famous for their skill, working at depths of 30 m (98 ft) or more.

### Japan’s Ama Divers

In Japan, **Ama divers** (often women) have collected shellfish, seaweed, and pearls for over 2,000 years. Their tradition continues today, with some Ama still diving into their 70s. Dives are usually 5-10 m (16-33 ft), but can reach 20 m (66 ft).

### Korea’s Haenyeo

Similar to the Ama, Korea’s **Haenyeo** (literally “sea women”) dive for abalone, octopus, and shellfish. They are renowned for communal work, songs, and rituals connected with the sea. Their practice is now UNESCO-recognised as intangible cultural heritage.

### Pacific Island Cultures

In the Pacific, freediving supported fishing and navigation. Polynesian divers harvested food and practised long-distance swimming and breath-holding as part of exploration traditions. Stories of **speardivers** and reef hunters remain central in many island cultures.

Freediving in Early Records
---------------------------

*   **Homer’s Iliad (8th century BCE/BC):** references warriors diving for sponges.
*   **Herodotus (5th century BCE/BC):** describes the diver Scyllis, who cut Persian naval anchors.
*   **2nd century CE/AD:** Oppian’s “Halieutica” refers to sponge diving as a profession.

These references confirm freediving was both common and essential long before it became a sport.

Are we Aquatic Apes?
--------------------

Some scientists suggest that humans may have evolved with a semi-aquatic phase — the so-called **Aquatic Ape Hypothesis**. The theory does not imagine gilled hybrids, but early hominids adapting to life in and around shallow water.

Wading upright would have freed the hands for gathering shellfish and seaweed while offering some protection from predators. A diet rich in protein and omega-3 oils may have supported rapid brain development.

Supporters point to several human traits unusual among primates:

*   A layer of subcutaneous fat that provides insulation in water.
*   Fingertips that wrinkle after immersion, improving grip underwater.
*   The **mammalian dive reflex**, which slows heart rate and helps conserve oxygen.

Studies also show that human eyes can adapt for underwater vision if trained early, and that infants display innate aquatic responses – closing the airway and instinctively paddling when submerged.

While the hypothesis remains debated, it highlights just how deeply water is woven into our biology and behaviour.

_Note: The Aquatic Ape Hypothesis is not universally accepted in evolutionary science. Many researchers argue that these traits can be explained by other evolutionary pathways. Still, the idea remains a popular lens for exploring our close connection to water._

Sponge Divers and The Birth Of Modern Diving
--------------------------------------------

One of the most remarkable episodes in freediving history took place in **July 1913**. A Greek sponge diver named **Giorgos Haggi Statti** (sometimes recorded as Stathis Chatzi) was asked by the Italian Navy to help recover the lost anchor of the battleship _Regina Margherita_ near the island of Karpathos.

Despite suffering from emphysema and partial deafness from years of diving injuries, Statti agreed. Using a **skandalopetra** stone for ballast and a rope tied around his waist, he descended between **77 and 88 m (253-289 ft)** and stayed down for roughly **three minutes**. Against the odds, he located the massive anchor and was hauled back to the surface.

His feat was later confirmed by Italian naval records in 2001. For his success, Statti received a reward of **£5 and lifetime permission to fish with dynamite** – a telling sign of the era’s attitudes toward both resource use and diver welfare.

Although this story captured headlines, freediving at the time remained a tool of survival and commerce rather than recreation. Divers battled cold, poor visibility, and equalisation difficulties. It took a series of technological breakthroughs to pave the way for freediving as a modern sport.

### Key Innovations That Changed Diving

*   **1927 – Jacques O’Marchal:** Designed the first mask that enclosed the nose, allowing divers to equalise ear pressure more easily.
*   **1933 – Louis de Corlieu:** Patented “swimming propellers,” the first recognisable fins. His design was later licensed to **Owen Churchill**, who mass-produced them in the United States.
*   **1938 – Maxime Forjot:** Filed a patent for a mask with a compressible rubber nose pocket, further improving equalisation.
*   **1940s – Owen Churchill:** Modified de Corlieu’s fins; the U.S. and British navies adopted them during WWII.
*   **1951 – Hugh Bradner:** Developed the first **neoprene wetsuit**, primarily for thermal protection. Though not immediately commercialised, it became the template for the dive and surf industries and was quickly taken up by the U.S. Navy during the Korean War.

### The Naples Wager – 1949

The pivotal moment for modern freediving came in **1949**. Italian Air Force captain **Raimondo Bucher** accepted a bet that he could reach **30 m (98 ft)** in the Bay of Naples. At the time, scientists believed his lungs would collapse under the pressure.

Bucher surfaced unharmed and 50,000 lire richer. More importantly, he had disproved prevailing medical opinion and demonstrated that humans could adapt safely to depth. This dive is widely regarded as the **birth of modern freediving as a sport**.

### From Innovation to Sport

Following Bucher’s success, freediving shifted rapidly from utility to passion. The 1950s and 60s saw the rise of a new generation of pioneers – **Bob Croft**, **Jacques Mayol**, and **Enzo Maiorca** – who pushed depth records, attracted media attention, and inspired scientific research. Their achievements brought freediving into the global consciousness and set the stage for the competitive sport we know today.

[![Image 1: Vintage Diving Mask](https://www.deeperblue.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/AdobeStock_65128374-700x465.jpeg.webp)](https://www.deeperblue.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/AdobeStock_65128374.jpeg)

Vintage Diving Mask

The Pioneers of Modern Freediving (20th Century)
------------------------------------------------

With Giorgos Haggi Statti’s legendary 1913 dive and Raimondo Bucher’s 1949 wager laying the groundwork, freediving entered a new era in the second half of the 20th century. What had once been a tool of survival or commerce began to transform into an organised pursuit of depth, distance, and personal challenge.

The decades that followed produced a cast of extraordinary individuals whose ambition, rivalry, and philosophy defined modern freediving.

### Enzo Maiorca – The Relentless Challenger

Italian diver **Enzo Maiorca** emerged in the 1960s as one of the first true freediving icons. A man of fiery temperament and competitive drive, he pushed record after record, breaking depth barriers and holding the world’s attention.

*   In **1960**, he achieved 45 m (148 ft), surpassing previous limits.
*   By **1988**, he had reached **101 m (331 ft)** in No Limits diving.

Maiorca embodied determination. His rivalry with Jacques Mayol was the stuff of legend, their contrasting styles making headlines and later inspiring the film _The Big Blue_.

### Jacques Mayol – The Philosopher of the Deep

French freediver **Jacques Mayol** brought a very different approach. A practitioner of yoga and meditation, he believed freediving was as much a spiritual practice as a physical one.

*   In **1976**, he became the first man to descend beyond **100 m (328 ft)**.
*   He advocated that humans retained evolutionary adaptations — such as the mammalian dive reflex — linking us to our aquatic past.

Mayol’s philosophy resonated widely. He portrayed freediving not just as a competitive sport but as a way to explore inner calm and connection to the ocean.

### Bob Croft – The American Depth Pioneer

Across the Atlantic, **Bob Croft**, a U.S. Navy submariner, was also rewriting limits. Experimenting with lung packing and equalisation techniques, he set world records in the 1960s, diving beyond **70 m (230 ft)**.

Croft’s work bridged science and sport. His dives informed physiological studies on lung capacity, oxygen management, and human adaptability at depth.

[![Image 2: Robert (Bob) Croft is the grandfather of USA Freediving and the first person to hold a freediving world record as a US athlete.](https://www.deeperblue.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/12/7353533_1449123788.6956-700x466.jpg.webp)](https://www.deeperblue.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/12/7353533_1449123788.6956.jpg)

Robert (Bob) Croft is the grandfather of USA Freediving and the first person to hold a freediving world record as a US athlete.

### Umberto Pelizzari – The All-Round Champion

Italian freediver **Umberto Pelizzari** dominated the 1980s and 1990s as the most versatile athlete of his generation. He set world records in nearly every discipline, from Constant Weight to Static Apnea. His deepest dives included **150 m (492 ft)** in No Limits (1999) and **131 m (430 ft)** in Variable Weight (2001), before his retirement.

Beyond records, Pelizzari co-founded **AIDA** in 1994, establishing freediving’s first international rulebook, and later created **Apnea Academy**, a training system that remains central to education and safety. Featured in the IMAX film _Ocean Men_ (2001), he became known as freediving’s intellectual ambassador, emphasising physiology, discipline, and safety.

[![Image 3: Valerio grassi and Umberto Pellizzari – 1991 Elba island freediving world record in constant and variable weight](https://www.deeperblue.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/Valerio-grassi-and-Umberto-Pellizzari-1991-Elba-island-freediving-world-record-in-constant-and-variable-weight-700x510.jpg.webp)](https://www.deeperblue.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/Valerio-grassi-and-Umberto-Pellizzari-1991-Elba-island-freediving-world-record-in-constant-and-variable-weight.jpg.webp)

Valerio grassi and Umberto Pellizzari – 1991 Elba island freediving world record in constant and variable weight

### Francisco “Pipin” Ferreras – The Cuban Showman

Cuban-born **Francisco “Pipin” Ferreras** rose to prominence in the 1990s as a specialist in No Limits diving. In **2000**, he set a record of **162 m (531 ft)**, confirming his reputation as one of the boldest figures of the era.

Ferreras’ rivalry with Umberto Pelizzari defined a generation, contrasting Pelizzari’s precise, scientific approach with his own raw bravado. His career was later overshadowed by tragedy when his wife and diving partner **Audrey Mestre** died in 2002 during a record attempt. The incident, widely covered in international media, led to greater scrutiny of safety standards in extreme freediving.

### Tanya Streeter – The Record-Breaking Woman

Born in the Cayman Islands and raised in Texas, **Tanya Streeter** redefined freediving in the early 2000s. On **17 August 2002**, she set a No Limits world record of **160 m (525 ft)** in Turks & Caicos, surpassing the men’s record under AIDA rules at the time.

Streeter went on to hold multiple records across disciplines, often eclipsing both women’s and men’s benchmarks. Her achievements brought freediving unprecedented media attention, and she later used her platform to promote **ocean conservation** and advocate for safe, ethical diving practices.

[![Image 4: Tanya Streeter on her Variable Weight World Record Dive](https://www.deeperblue.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Tanya-Streeter-700x391.jpg.webp)](https://www.deeperblue.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Tanya-Streeter.jpg.webp)

Tanya Streeter on her Variable Weight World Record Dive

### Natalia Molchanova – A New Standard for Women

From 2002 until her disappearance in 2015, **Natalia Molchanova** redefined what was possible in freediving. She set more than **40 world records**, became the first woman to pass **100 m (328 ft)** in constant weight, and built a reputation as both champion and teacher.

Her technical mastery and calm authority made her the sport’s most respected ambassador, inspiring a generation of athletes.

[![Image 5: Natalia Molchanova after her Constant Weight No Fins (CNF) World Record in May 2014](https://www.deeperblue.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/05/10342920_10152145451013753_8655139402762152667_n-700x464.jpg.webp)](https://www.deeperblue.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/05/10342920_10152145451013753_8655139402762152667_n.jpg.webp)

Natalia Molchanova after her Constant Weight No Fins (CNF) World Record in May 2014

### Legacy of an Era

The rivalries of **Maiorca and Mayol**, the scientific insights of **Croft**, the all-round excellence of **Pelizzari**, the drama of **Pipin**, the barrier-breaking feats of Streeter, and the dominance of **Molchanova** defined the 20th century.

Together, they transformed freediving from daring stunts into a structured sport with formal rules, training systems, and safety standards. Their influence shaped freediving’s identity — balancing ambition with responsibility — and set the stage for the contemporary champions who continue to push human limits today.

### Contemporary Champions

The torch lit by Mayol, Maiorca, Croft, and Molchanova has been carried forward by a new generation of freedivers who continue to push human limits.

*   **Herbert Nitsch (Austria)**  
    Known as _“The Deepest Man on Earth,”_ Herbert Nitsch has achieved **33 world records** across nearly every freediving discipline. His most famous dive came on **14 June 2007**, when he descended to **214 m (702 ft)** in the No Limits (NLT) category off Spetses, Greece — still the deepest officially recognised dive in history.In 2012, Nitsch attempted an unprecedented **253 m (831 ft)**. Severe decompression injuries prevented official ratification, but the attempt cemented his place as one of the boldest figures in freediving history.
*   **William Trubridge (New Zealand)**  
    A specialist in **Constant Weight No Fins (CNF)** – often regarded as the sport’s purest and most demanding discipline – Trubridge became the first diver to break the **100 m (328 ft)** barrier in CNF in 2010. He later pushed the CNF record to **102 m (334 ft)** in July 2016 at Dean’s Blue Hole, Bahamas.His achievement stood until **May 2025**, when Croatia’s **Petar Klovar** reached **103 m (338 ft)**. Beyond records, Trubridge has been a tireless advocate for safety, ocean conservation, and raising freediving’s profile on the world stage.
*   **Alexey Molchanov (Russia)**  
    Son of the late Natalia Molchanova, Alexey has become the **most decorated freediver in history**, with over **40 world records** across multiple disciplines.  
    – **Constant Weight (CWT):** In 2023, he reached **136 m (446 ft)** in Limassol, Cyprus – the deepest CWT dive ever.  
    – **Constant Weight with Bifins (CWTB):** Multiple records beyond **120 m (394 ft)**.  
    – **Free Immersion (FIM):** Holds several of the world’s deepest performances.  
    As of 2025, Molchanov remains the undisputed leader in depth disciplines, continuing to push the boundaries of human physiology and technique.

Together, these contemporary champions highlight how far freediving has progressed in only a few decades. Where scientists once believed depths beyond 30 m were fatal, athletes today regularly exceed 100 m (328 ft) with refined technique, training, and safety protocols.

[![Image 6: William Trubridge At Deans Blue Hole](https://www.deeperblue.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/04/William_Trubridge-169-700x467.jpg.webp)](https://www.deeperblue.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/04/William_Trubridge-169.jpg.webp)

William Trubridge At Deans Blue Hole

### Latest Highlights (2023-2025)

*   **CNF: Petar Klovar (Croatia)** – 103 m (338 ft), May 2025.
*   **CWT: Alexey Molchanov (Russia)** – 136 m (446 ft), 2023 (still standing).
*   **No Limits: Herbert Nitsch (Austria)** – 214 m (702 ft), 2007 (unbeaten).

A Timeline of Freediving Milestones
-----------------------------------

*   **~3000 BCE – Ancient Mediterranean:** Sponge and pearl divers recorded in early Greek and Middle Eastern sources.
*   **8th century BCE – Homer’s Iliad:** Mentions warriors diving for sponges during the Trojan War.
*   **5th century BCE – Scyllis of Scione:** According to Herodotus, the Greek diver sabotaged the Persian fleet by cutting anchor lines underwater.
*   **1913 – Giorgos Haggi Statti (Greece):** Descended between 77-88 m (253-289 ft) to recover the Italian battleship Regina Margherita’s lost anchor near Karpathos.
*   **1949 – Raimondo Bucher (Italy):** Won a wager by diving to 30 m (98 ft) in Naples Bay, disproving claims that such depths were fatal.
*   **1960s – Enzo Maiorca (Italy):** Repeatedly broke depth records, surpassing 50 m (164 ft) and pushing freediving into public view.
*   **1976 – Jacques Mayol (France):** Became the first person to reach 100 m (328 ft), combining yoga and meditation with technique.
*   **1988 – Enzo Maiorca:** Returned to the spotlight with a dive to 101 m (331 ft).
*   **1960s-70s – Bob Croft (USA):** U.S. Navy submariner set records beyond 70 m (230 ft), contributing to physiological research.
*   **2002-2015 – Natalia Molchanova (Russia):** Set over 40 world records, first woman beyond 100 m (328 ft), widely regarded as the greatest female freediver.
*   **2007 – Herbert Nitsch (Austria):** Achieved 214 m (702 ft) in No Limits off Spetses, Greece — the deepest officially recognised dive.
*   **2010 – William Trubridge (New Zealand):** First diver to break 100 m (328 ft) in Constant Weight No Fins (CNF).
*   **2016 – William Trubridge:** Extended CNF record to 102 m (334 ft) at Dean’s Blue Hole.
*   **2023 – Alexey Molchanov (Russia):** Set the Constant Weight (CWT) record at 136 m (446 ft) in Cyprus.
*   **2025 – Petar Klovar (Croatia):** Set a new CNF record of 103 m (338 ft), surpassing Trubridge.

Science and Physiology
----------------------

The mid-20th century brought scientific insight into freediving:

*   **Mammalian Dive Reflex** was studied, showing bradycardia and blood shift as adaptations.
*   **Equalization techniques** such as Frenzel and Mouthfill were refined.
*   **Understanding of barotrauma and squeezes** improved training safety.

This combination of science and sport transformed freediving into a modern, legitimate discipline rather than a dangerous stunt.

Freediving Today
----------------

Freediving is now practiced globally:

*   **Recreational freedivers** explore reefs, wrecks, and caves.
*   **Competitive freedivers** train for world championships under organisations like AIDA and CMAS.
*   **Underwater photographers and filmmakers** use freediving for natural interaction with marine life.
*   **Traditional communities** (Ama, Haenyeo, Polynesian divers) continue their heritage.

The sport grows every year, supported by courses, clubs, and scientific research.

FAQs
----

### Who was the first person to dive 100 m?

Jacques Mayol in 1976, at Elba, Italy.

### Who is considered the greatest freediver?

Many regard Natalia Molchanova as the greatest, with over 40 world records and unmatched influence as an athlete and teacher.

### Why are Italy and France so important in freediving history?

They produced many early pioneers (Maiorca, Mayol) and hosted record-setting dives that shaped the sport’s development.

### What is the deepest freedive ever recorded?

Herbert Nitsch’s 214 m (702 ft) No Limits dive in 2007 remains the deepest officially recognised dive.

Continuing Education Activity
-----------------------------

Open-circuit self-contained underwater breathing apparatus (SCUBA) has been used by recreational, scientific, exploration, and military divers since Cousteau and Gagnon introduced the technology shortly after World War II. In contrast, closed-circuit rebreathers predate open-circuit systems, originating in basic forms as early as the 1800s. Closed-circuit breathing apparatus, known as rebreathers, reuse exhaled gas after scrubbing carbon dioxide and replenishing oxygen, offering greater efficiency but necessitating sophisticated monitoring and management. Due to their complexity, rebreathers present unique physiological and operational challenges that healthcare providers must recognize when managing diving-related incidents, particularly those related to gas toxicity, hypoxia, and hypercapnia. This activity explores the operational principles of diving rebreathers, highlighting their advantages and risks in comparison to traditional open-circuit SCUBA systems. In addition, the activity reviews critical safety considerations and emergency response procedures required when treating divers who experience complications related to rebreather use. The activity also emphasizes the importance of interprofessional teamwork, underscoring collaboration among healthcare providers, diving specialists, and emergency responders to optimize outcomes in diving medicine.

**Objectives:**

*   Identify the different types of rebreathers used in diving activities.
    
*   Assess clinical concerns that are associated with SCUBA diving activities.
    
*   Screen for signs and symptoms of diving-related complications specific to rebreather use during patient assessment.
    
*   Collaborate with the interprofessional team to coordinate care and enhance the safety of individuals using rebreathers during diving activities.
    

[Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.](https://www.statpearls.com/account/trialuserreg/?articleid=31573&utm_source=pubmed&utm_campaign=reviews&utm_content=31573)

Introduction
------------

Open-circuit self-contained underwater breathing apparatus (SCUBA) has been used by recreational, exploration, scientific, and military divers since the advent of the technology by Cousteau and Gagnon shortly after World War II. At the most fundamental level, an underwater breathing apparatus can be delineated into surface-supplied and self-contained units. Surface-supplied divers use an umbilical to provide breathing gas to the diver, whereas SCUBA divers always carry their life support equipment with them. SCUBA systems are further classified as open-circuit or closed-circuit types. Open-circuit dive equipment provides the diver with breathing gas from a container (or tank) of compressed gas, allowing the diver to exhale directly into the environment. Although simple and easy to maintain, this system is inefficient, as a large volume of inert gas is exhaled to the environment, and a substantial amount of oxygen remains unused. With a closed-circuit breathing apparatus, commonly known as a rebreather, exhaled gas is collected, carbon dioxide is removed, oxygen is replenished, and the refreshed gas is recirculated back to the diver through a breathing loop. The oxygen consumed by the diver through metabolic consumption is the only thing that must be replaced to continue to sustain the diver, whereas carbon dioxide must be removed. This system is inherently more efficient, up to 50 times more efficient for a given gas supply, but also more complex, requiring constant monitoring of the gas in the system to ensure it can sustain life.[\[1\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482469/#article-31573.r1)

Rebreathers have been used since ancient times, when humans first discovered that they could extend the duration of a free dive by breathing in and out of a leather bag. Over 100 years ago, more sophisticated models were developed to allow miners to escape from contaminated atmospheric conditions and were used with varying degrees of success. During World War II, rebreather technology was adapted to enable combat divers to operate in enemy harbors without releasing surface bubbles that could reveal their position. The challenges associated with rebreathers include the potential for hypercarbia, oxygen toxicity, and hypoxia.[\[2\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482469/#article-31573.r2) Before more technically advanced devices became available in the 1980s and 1990s, blackouts due to various gas problems were a common complication.[\[3\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482469/#article-31573.r3) In the 1990s, several commercial units became available on the civilian market, leading to a significant increase in civilian diver use in the early 2000s. Today, a wide variety of rebreather systems is available, designed to meet the diverse demands of various diving environments and applications.

Function
--------

Rebreathers are categorized based on how they add gases, particularly oxygen, to the breathing loop. There are various types of rebreathers, including semi-closed circuit rebreathers with active or passive addition mechanisms and fully closed circuit rebreathers with manual or electronically controlled oxygen addition. Some hybrid units incorporate multiple oxygen addition mechanisms.

**Fundamental Rebreather Design**

All rebreathers share fundamental similarities dictated by the physical principles that govern their function. Each unit includes a scrubber to remove exhaled carbon dioxide and a counterlung—a flexible reservoir that allows the diver to inhale and exhale underwater, as breathing into a rigid, sealed container is not possible. Rebreathers typically have one-way valves installed in the breathing loop to direct gas flow into and out of the unit, preventing a diver from rebreathing gas that has not been scrubbed of carbon dioxide. All commercially available rebreathers have sensor systems that monitor the partial pressure of oxygen to prevent divers from breathing hypoxic or hyperoxic gas mixtures. Depending on the model, rebreathers have 1 or more gas supply bottles to supply fresh gas to the diver. Some rebreathers bleed oxygen-enriched mixtures into the counterlung, whereas others monitor the oxygen levels available to the diver and bleed pure oxygen into the system to compensate for the oxygen depleted by the diver's metabolic needs. As both the diver's lungs and the counterlung on the rebreather are subject to compression with descent due to the effects described by Boyle's law, all rebreathers have a mechanism to inject gas into the breathing loop to counter the effects of volume loss with increased pressure. As pure oxygen becomes toxic at relatively shallow depths, rebreathers containing pure oxygen typically include a diluent gas to compensate for volume loss without risking oxygen toxicity. Various military organizations worldwide use shallow-water pure oxygen rebreathers with single-gas supplies due to their specific needs and advantages. Many rebreathers use retention straps to maintain airway protection during hyperoxic seizures.

**Semi-Closed Circuit Rebreathers:** Semi-closed circuit rebreathers continuously add breathing gas to the loop through a constant mass flow orifice and vent exhaled gas from the loop every few exhalations. Using this passive system, typically controlled by the diver's breathing, the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) in the breathing loop is generally maintained within 2% to 3% of a preselected amount. The system is simple and highly reliable; early units were sold without oxygen monitoring equipment. However, there are notable limitations; the FiO2 is designed for a diver workload within a specific range, and hypoxia can occur with unexpectedly high workloads. As most systems vent approximately one-fifth of each breath, the volume of the counterlung varies, and diver buoyancy is affected. Currently, this system is seldom used due to the availability of more advanced units with far greater depth and duration capability. Semi-closed units had simpler designs and training, making them desirable to some divers during the early days of rebreather use in the nonmilitary community.

**Closed-Circuit Rebreathers:** Closed-circuit rebreathers are available in various designs and use multiple oxygen addition mechanisms. These rebreathers are typically delineated based on their oxygen addition mechanism. The most common types include the manually controlled closed-circuit rebreather, the electronically controlled closed-circuit rebreather, and the hybrid closed-circuit rebreather, which combines features of both manually and electronically controlled rebreathers. Each model has advantages and limitations.

Manual closed-circuit rebreathers are common and rely upon the diver to maintain the partial pressure of oxygen in the breathing loop. In their most basic form, the diver must manually inject oxygen with a button and monitor the partial loop pressure of oxygen using a series of sensors. If the diver fails to act with this system, oxygen is not supplied, and the diver eventually becomes hypoxic. Due to the dire consequences of failing to act, the diver is forced to pay close attention to the unit, and as a result, most commercial units appear to have a good safety record. A more common variation of this unit involves manual oxygen addition through a button, where oxygen bleeds into the loop at a very slow rate to match the diver's resting metabolic rate. Because there is a small constant addition of oxygen, the diver may only need to add oxygen every 10 to 15 minutes at rest, reducing the diver's workload. The oxygen in this system is injected through a constant mass flow restricted orifice. Because the orifice is sonic, once drive pressure is set, typically around 160 psi, the mass of oxygen injected over any given period is constant, regardless of depth. This drive pressure also limits the diving depth, as the unit stops injecting oxygen at a depth corresponding to the drive pressure, which typically ranges from 250 to 360 feet of water. The combination of passive constant oxygen flow and manual injection represents the design of most manually controlled closed-circuit rebreathers currently available.

Electronic closed-circuit rebreathers inject oxygen through a magnetic solenoid and a computer that monitors the oxygen levels in the loop, automatically injecting a bolus of oxygen to compensate for diver usage. These systems are fully automated; support unlimited depth, as the oxygen first stage does not require presetting at a specific pressure; and are highly efficient in oxygen usage. Some argue that fully automatic systems can lead to the diver becoming complacent about monitoring their oxygen levels, potentially delaying the detection of critical gas supply issues. There is evidence supporting this theory, especially when electronically controlled closed-circuit rebreathers were first introduced to the civilian market.[\[4\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482469/#article-31573.r4) Recent evidence suggests that the accident rates between electronically controlled closed-circuit rebreathers and manual systems are comparable.[\[5\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482469/#article-31573.r5) What is not in debate is that complex electronics immersed in saltwater have a higher failure rate than the simple mechanical push-button valves found on manually controlled closed-circuit rebreathers, and solenoids and computers require electricity to operate, whereas mechanical valves do not. Some divers use electronically controlled closed-circuit rebreathers manually while using a slightly lower oxygen set point on the computer, which then serves as a reserve parachute and kicks in if the diver fails to add oxygen. This system assumes that the likelihood of a diver becoming distracted at the exact moment the electronics fail is minimal. Some divers who preferred to operate electronically controlled closed-circuit rebreathers manually added a constant mass flow orifice to their systems, thereby significantly extending the time before needing to add additional oxygen. This innovation led to the development of the hybrid closed-circuit rebreather, which is now available as a variant of several commercial electronically controlled closed-circuit rebreathers.

Issues of Concern
-----------------

Rebreathers are associated with increased complexity and potential for error compared to open-circuit dive equipment; however, they offer additional benefits for operational divers, including reduced gas utilization, increased bottom time, and the ability to perform stealthy excursions. In underwater exploration, unexpected events can prolong a dive, particularly at its maximum depth. Traditionally, this unexpected time has resulted in the depletion of emergency gas supplies and an increased incidence of near misses and fatalities. A rebreather can significantly reduce the time pressure on the diver, as it can extend dive time by several hours if needed, allowing the diver to address problems such as getting lost, clearing an entanglement, finding a lost buddy, or dealing with unexpected environmental challenges.[\[6\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482469/#article-31573.r6) In reality, the use of mixed-gas rebreathers has been documented as enabling divers to address these issues. However, it is still associated with higher fatality rates compared to traditional open-circuit SCUBA.[\[5\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482469/#article-31573.r5) This apparent disparity is most easily explained by the types of dives undertaken with this apparatus. Rebreather-equipped divers undertake dives that either are not possible on traditional open-circuit SCUBA or are logistically challenging, requiring multiple setup dives to stage safety gas bottles before the dive. This situation may be somewhat analogous to the introduction of jet aircraft—higher and faster flights became possible, connecting cities in hours instead of days, but the crashes were initially more spectacular as well. Additional safety innovations, such as the development of carbon dioxide (CO2) monitors that function reliably in 100% humidity environments and advancements in scrubber bed monitoring technology, may help mitigate the risks associated with rebreather use.[\[7\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482469/#article-31573.r7)[\[8\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482469/#article-31573.r8) Rebreathers offer advantages in terms of increased depth and duration compared to traditional open-circuit equipment.

Clinical Significance
---------------------

Divers using rebreathers are subject to additional risks for oxygen toxicity, hypoxia, and hypercarbia beyond those associated with traditional open-circuit SCUBA.[\[7\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482469/#article-31573.r7) These divers are also susceptible to all forms of decompression illness, including decompression sickness and overexpansion injuries, that an open-circuit diver can get. Carbon dioxide absorbents are also limited in their ability to bind CO2, and this limitation also functionally limits the time the rebreather can be used without replenishment. The finite scrubbing capacity creates a situation where a diver may have gas, but the rebreather may no longer be able to effectively scrub CO2 from the loop once the sorb is exhausted. Although temperature sensors can be used to monitor the effective life of a scrubber, they are imperfect and only provide an estimation of time remaining based on the current workload of the diver.[\[6\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482469/#article-31573.r6) In addition, the material that removes CO2 from the breathing loop is highly caustic (sodium hydroxide has a pH of nearly 14) and forms a strong base when mixed with water. Although most modern commercial rebreathers have water traps of various designs to help prevent this caustic material from being ingested or inhaled if the breathing loop is inadvertently flooded, this can not typically be wholly prevented. If a diver inhales or ingests this caustic material, known as a caustic cocktail to divers, the mouth should be thoroughly irrigated with freshwater, and the diver should be evaluated for a caustic burn. The diver should never be instructed to drink acidic fluids, as the resultant exothermic reaction can be clinically significant. Airway compromise can occur from the ingestion of a caustic cocktail.[\[9\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482469/#article-31573.r9) Consultation with a toxicologist, pulmonologist, or hyperbaric physician trained in undersea medicine is recommended.

Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
----------------------------------

Divers using rebreathers are subject to additional risks for oxygen toxicity, hypoxia, and hypercarbia beyond those associated with traditional open-circuit SCUBA. These divers are also susceptible to all forms of decompression illness, including decompression sickness and overexpansion injuries, that an open-circuit diver can get. Carbon dioxide absorbents are also limited in their ability to bind CO2, and this limitation also functionally limits the time the rebreather can be used without replenishment. The key to preventing these injuries is education. Healthcare professionals, including diving medical technicians, hyperbaric nurses, and physician hyperbaric specialists, should educate patients on the dangers of deep-sea diving, such as decompression sickness, and potential risks associated with using rebreathers.

![Image 1: commercial divers underwater working](https://asi-group.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/GOPR0022-scaled-e1657111227247-800x600.jpg)

### And how does it differ from Scuba diving?

Commercial diving is a type of professional diving where the diver engages in underwater work for industrial, construction, engineering, maintenance or other commercial purposes.

The fundamental difference between commercial diving and scuba diving is scuba divers use breathing equipment not dependent on an air supply from the surface. In fact, SCUBA is an acronym for _Self-Contained Underwater Breathing Apparatus._ A commercial diver is directly attached to a surface-supplied diving system which uses umbilical or hoses connected to their helmet from a gas supply on the surface.

ASI’s commercial divers tend to work in challenging and sometimes extreme environments that can have very serious risks. In addition to the possibilities of drowning or hypothermia, they are exposed to physical injuries from underwater equipment and structures. Pressure related injuries such as barotrauma (lungs, middle ear, sinuses), decompression sickness (The Bends) and embolisms can cause damage and even death. Divers sometimes work in water with low visibility and little to no light. Working in and around dams or any structure with a water intake means no diving unless there’s a shutdown; but if there’s an abnormality in the structure of a dam wall, a loss of integrity can prove fatal for a diver.

#### **Commercial diving is one of the riskiest occupations in the world**

To mitigate these risks, commercial divers are not only trained and certified in what they do, but they must plan and assess the work and environment before anyone enters the water. A detailed risk assessment called a Hazard Assessment Safety and Environmental Plan, or HASEP, is completed and pre-dive meetings are held with the crew. All dive operations are carried out in accordance with Canadian Diving Standards and Provincial Regulations. Diving crews include, at **minimum,** four trained and qualified personnel (a diver, a diving supervisor, tender and stand-by diver). Once onsite the crew works together to ensure equipment is checked and the diver is suited up correctly.

![Image 2](https://asi-group.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Surface.supply.diving.configuration.png)

Surface Supply Diving Configuration

The diver’s equipment is specialized too. The suit they wear (called a drysuit) provides them with insulation and as the name suggests, keeps them dry. Typically, a commercial diver’s equipment includes a weight belt for buoyancy control, a safety harness, a secondary source for air as back up in the case of an emergency, a knife, LED lighting and a camera. They are also hard-wired for communication so the dive supervisor on site is always in contact with the diver.

ASI uses commercial divers for underwater construction, inspections, maintenance and repairs for intakes and outfalls, bridges, dams, docks, ports, piers and more. Commercial divers are used to facilitate maintenance at nuclear facilities, and they provide inspection and repair services to ships within the Great Lakes region and on the West Coast in BC.

If you want to learn more about what our [**commercial divers**](https://asi-group.com/commercial-diving/) can do, [**contact us today**](mailto:info@asi-group.com?subject=Commercial%20Diving%20Services).

Have you ever wondered how people can dive into deep water for long periods of time without any breathing apparatus? Or maybe you have questioned whether there are actually any differences between freediving and snorkeling? Despite your knowledge of the sport, you’re bound to have some questions before you take the plunge to become a [PADI Freediver™.](https://www.padi.com/education/freediving/) Here are the answers to some of the most commonly asked questions about learning to freedive.

#### What Is Freediving?

Diving into deep waters on one breath and without any breathing apparatus is referred to as ‘freediving’. Freedivers use inward control, discipline and power to descend into the ocean while holding their breath until they resurface. Freediving is both a recreational and competitive sport, with many freediving competitions being held regularly around the world.

![Image 1: PADI Freediver - Open Water Freedive](https://blog.padi.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/FdiverAug2015_0962_resize.jpg)

#### What Is the Difference Between Snorkeling and Freediving?

Although both freediving and snorkeling require the use of similar equipment, the two activities are quite different. Snorkelers remain on the surface of the ocean looking down with their mask while breathing through their snorkels. Whereas, freedivers dive deep beneath the ocean’s surface holding their breath until they resurface. Freedivers only use their snorkel at the surface of the water and instead, remove this piece of equipment before they descend.

#### If I Can’t Hold My Breath for a Long Time Does That Mean I Can’t Freedive?

This is one of the most common misconceptions about freediving. With proper training you will learn breath-hold techniques that will likely result in you being pleasantly surprised by how long you can hold your breath.

#### Do I Need to Know How to Swim?

While you don’t need to be an Olympic swimmer to take the course, it is important that you feel confident in the water. To become a PADI Freediver you will need to be able to swim 200 meters/218 yards. This swim will be untimed and can be completed using any stroke, so you can take your time. You’ll also need to learn multiple breath-hold techniques, some of which involve swimming underwater and at depth.

![Image 2: PADI Freediver - Confined Water Freedive - Dynamic Apnea](https://blog.padi.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/FdiverAug2015_0580-Copy.jpg)

#### How Old Do I Need to Be to Start Freediving?

To enrol in the PADI Freediver course you must be at least 15 years old. However, if you’re younger than 15 years old but want to learn how to freedive, we have modified courses available. Those aged 12 years or older can enrol in the [PADI Basic Freediver](https://store.padi.com/en-us/ns/courses/basic-freediver/p/basic-freediver/) course and anyone aged 8 years of age or older can start their [PADI Skin Diver](https://store.padi.com/en-us/ns/courses/skin-diver/p/skin-diver/) course.

#### How Long Does It Take to Get Certified?

PADI courses are constructed so that the required skills can be mastered irrespective of set time periods. Some people may find these skills easier to achieve while others may need a little more time. Despite your natural ability, the PADI Freediver course will ensure that you’re equipped with the appropriate skills needed to safely freedive.

#### What Are the Course Requirements?

To become a PADI Freediver you will need to complete three main phases of the course:

1.  **Knowledge Development** – This is the theory portion of the course that you will need to complete before you start your confined and open water sessions. You can complete this independent study either through PADI Freediver eLearning or classroom sessions with your [PADI Freediver Instructor](https://store.padi.com/en-us/ns/courses/freediver/p/freediver/-instructor).
2.  **Confined Water Sessions** – During this section of your course you will learn multiple breath-hold techniques in order to achieve a static apnea of 90 seconds and a dynamic apnea of 25 meters/80 feet.
3.  **Open Water Sessions** – This is where you will practice your breath-hold techniques during both free immersion and constant weight freedives to 10 meters/30 feet. You will also complete a range of buddy and safety procedures.

![Image 3: PADI Freediver - Constant Weight - Open Water Freedive](https://blog.padi.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/FdiverAug2015_0129_resize.jpg)

#### What Are the Different Types of Freediving?

There are four different types of freediving that you will practice during your PADI Freediving course.

1.  **Static Apnea** – This discipline requires the diver to hold their breath for as long as possible while floating face down in confined water. The diver’s respiratory tracts must be submerged during this activity.
2.  **Dynamic Apnea** – In confined water, divers will need to swim in a horizontal position underwater to cover the greatest distance possible. This discipline can be performed as either a fins or no fins activity.
3.  **Free Immersion** – During this discipline the diver will use the guided rope to propel themselves down as far as they can and then back up to the surface. This activity can also be performed with or without fins.
4.  **Constant Weight** – In this activity divers use control and power to push themselves down as far as they can next to the guided rope. During this discipline the diver is not allowed to touch the guided rope. Performed in open water, divers can either complete this activity with or without fins.

#### Do I Need My Own Freediving Equipment?

Not at all. Freedivers only require a few equipment items; mask, snorkel, fins, weight belt (if required) and wetsuit (depending on you’re location), so most [PADI Freediver™ Centers](https://www.padi.com/freediver-centers) will have gear available for hire. Of course as your love for the sport develops, you may decide to purchase your own equipment.

Are you ready to start experiencing the underwater world on one breath? Find out more information about the [PADI Freediver course](https://store.padi.com/en-us/ns/courses/freediver/p/freediver/) and contact your local [PADI Freediver Center](https://www.padi.com/freediver-centers) today!

[What is scuba diving?](https://store.padi.com/en-us/education/learn-to-dive/) Explained briefly, [scuba diving](https://www.padi.com/) is a water sport that involves breathing air from a tank while underwater. [Scuba](https://www.padi.com/) is an acronym for **S**elf **C**ontained **U**nderwater **B**reathing **A**pparatus. Most [scuba divers](https://store.padi.com/en-us/education/learn-to-dive/) are recreational divers who explore underwater environments such as lakes, rivers, quarries, kelp forests and coral reefs. There are also people who [scuba dive](https://www.padi.com/) [for work](https://blog.padi.com/top-7-jobs-for-scuba-divers/) including [public safety divers](https://blog.padi.com/2013/04/23/publicsafetydiver_interview/), [marine biologists](https://blog.padi.com/becoming-marine-biologist-imke-mayer/) and many others. Start your [scuba diving adventure here](https://store.padi.com/en-us/courses/open-water-diver/p/60462-1B2C/).

* * *

![Image 1](https://blog.padi.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/PADI-scuba-divers-scaled.jpg)

How is scuba diving done? 
--------------------------

There’s more to [scubadiving](https://www.padi.com/) than just knowing the scuba [diving meaning](https://www.scubadiving.com/training/decompression-diving), strapping a tank on your back and jumping in the water. It all starts with a dive plan.

You might choose the dive site and invite friends, or a dive buddy might message you, “Conditions are going to be great this weekend!” Either way, your plan should include diving with at least one other person in case anything goes wrong underwater. If you don’t have a dive buddy, the local [dive shop](https://apps.padi.com/scuba-diving/dive-shop-locator/) can help you find one.

Once you decide where you want to dive and for how long, you’ll choose the appropriate scuba equipment. For example:

*   If you plan to make multiple dives, you’ll want extra scuba tanks.
*   When diving in cold water, many divers wear a [dry suit](https://www.padi.com/gear/dry-suits) instead of a wetsuit to stay warm.
*   If the dive site is a [shore dive](https://blog.padi.com/best-shore-diving-destinations/), you may need a [dive float](https://www.padi.com/gear/flags).

Many divers own their own [scuba gear](https://www.padi.com/gear) and either rent tanks or get their tanks filled at a local shop. Others rent all their diving equipment. Watch this video to learn more about [how scuba gear works](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Sc99x5RKlh8).

When the dive day arrives, you’ll check the dive conditions one more time. If everything looks good, you’ll head to the dock or dive site with your gear.

* * *

What is scuba diving like? 
---------------------------

It’s hard to explain [what scuba diving feels like](https://blog.padi.com/what-is-scuba-diving-like/) for [scuba divers underwater](http://www.scubadiving.com/home). The best way to find out is to try it for yourself. If you’re not ready to enroll in a scuba certification class, try a [Discover Scuba Diving](https://store.padi.com/en-us/ns/courses/discover-scuba-diving/p/discover-scuba-diving/)**®** Experience. In a pool or calm water environment, you’ll take your first breaths underwater under the guidance of a PADI Scuba Instructor or Divemaster.

A Discover Scuba Experience allows you to [try scuba diving](https://travel.padi.com/padi-courses-locator/all/?courses=36) under the guidance of a dive professional, but if you want to dive independently with your friends, you’ll need a [scuba certification](https://www.padi.com/education/learn-to-dive). In a scuba certification course, you learn basic scuba skills, safety procedures and other essentials.

A PADI® [Open Water Diver](https://store.padi.com/en-us/courses/open-water-diver/p/60462-1B2C/) certification is the world’s most recognized scuba certification. Watch the video above to learn [how to get scuba certified](https://blog.padi.com/how-to-become-a-scuba-diver-everything-you-want-to-know/). Or read about the [difference between Discover Scuba Diving and Open Water Diver](https://blog.padi.com/discover-scuba-diving-and-open-water-whats-the-difference/).

* * *

Who can scuba dive?
-------------------

Scuba diving is open to anyone eight years old or older who is comfortable in the water. At age ten, kids can earn a Junior Open Water certification. There is no upper age limit.

To learn to dive you must have basic swimming skills and no [underlying health conditions](https://www.padi.com/sites/default/files/documents/2020-08/10346E_Diver_Medical_Form.pdf). People of all abilities can scuba dive, including individuals with paraplegia, amputations, or other physical challenges.

Is scuba diving safe?
---------------------

With the right training, scuba diving is considerably safer than other popular activities. [Statistics show](https://blog.padi.com/scuba-diving-safe/) you’re more likely to get injured fishing, playing golf, snowboarding or even bowling than scuba diving. The most common medical issues associated with [diving scuba](http://www.scubadiving.com/home) are sunburn, [seasickness](https://blog.padi.com/simple-tips-for-preventing-seasickness-divers-alert-network/), and dehydration (all of which are preventable).

One of the biggest [myths about scuba diving](https://blog.padi.com/top-10-scuba-diving-myths/) safety has to do with sharks. The truth is, in a [list of animals most deadly to humans](https://blog.padi.com/18-things-dangerous-sharks/), sharks don’t even rank in the top 10. There are [more than 500 species of sharks](https://ocean.si.edu/ocean-life/sharks-rays/sharks) and very few are ever aggressive toward humans.

As a scuba diver, you’ll start to see things through new eyes. Most divers think sharks are captivating creatures, not something to be feared!

* * *

Experience Life Unfiltered
--------------------------

Scuba diving is one of the few experiences where you can see fascinating animals in their natural habitat – authentic and [unfiltered](https://www.padi.com/live-unfiltered). When you immerse yourself in the world beneath the waves, you leave text messages and to-do lists behind. It’s the perfect escape from the demands of the surface world.

Are You Interested in Learning To Scuba Dive?
---------------------------------------------

If you’re curious about learning how to scuba dive, you can start your scuba lessons online for free. [Click here to demo the online course](https://www.padi.com/dive/free-intro-open-water-course) and learn about underwater hand signals and the critical role divers play in ocean protection. Or for more information on learning to dive, including how to sign up for your PADI Open Water Diver course, click below.

* * *

Go Deeper 
----------

*   [7 Signs It’s Time To Become a Diver](https://blog.padi.com/5-signs-its-time-to-become-a-diver/)
*   [Snorkeling vs. Scuba Diving – What’s the Difference?](https://blog.padi.com/snorkeling-vs-scuba-diving/)
*   [Scuba Diving for Kids](https://blog.padi.com/scuba-diving-lessons-for-kids/)
